content:
Do you remember Google I/O in the summer of 2014?

Android was just climbing out of the clunky, utilitarian ditch of versions 2.3 and 4.0, while the entire tech industry was still marveling at the clean, flat look of Apple’s iOS 7. Right at that pivotal moment, Matías Duarte walked onto the stage in his famously loud patterned shirt and unveiled Material Design.

Photo: Matías Duarte announcing Material Design, Google's ambitious new visual language, at Google I/O 2014.

The keynote was staged like high theater. From virtual paper and digital ink to quantum materials and diffuse light reflection, Google went so far as to calculate initial physical velocities for touch-ripple animations. The official blog followed up with a line that echoed across Silicon Valley: “One consistent design that spans devices”—a singular design language uniting mobile, tablet, desktop, and the web. Back then, designers and developers in the audience listened with racing pulses, genuinely convinced that Google was drafting a self-consistent physics for the digital world and ending the wild-west era of Android once and for all.

Image: Early Material Design concepts and application mocks showcased at Google I/O 2014.

And what came of it? Twelve years later, what kind of report card has this supposedly universal design system actually turned in?

Samsung, which ships the overwhelming majority of the world's Android hardware, completely ignored Google’s latest Material 3 Expressive push in One UI 8, choosing instead to copy Apple’s translucent frosted glass pixel for pixel. WhatsApp and Telegram, used by billions every day, have spent four straight years refusing to even look at Google’s heavily hyped “wallpaper dynamic color extraction.” Inside Google’s own house, Gmail, Docs, and Sheets were rocking sharp rectangular drawers a decade ago and are still rocking sharp rectangular drawers today. YouTube carved out its own fiefdom with a custom black-and-red UI and ignored the spec entirely. Over in the open-source world, the official libraries for iOS and the web were officially abandoned years ago, and even Google's beloved cross-platform framework Flutter spent 2026 scrambling to rip Material out of its core SDK to keep its distance.

A globe-spanning empire that promised universal consistency over twelve long years has retreated into what? A local sandbox propped up by Pixel phones, a handful of system settings screens, and a suite of proprietary internal frameworks.

This isn't a matter of "design is subjective" or "a noble artistic exploration." From start to finish, Material Design has been textbook Silicon Valley corporate self-indulgence: mediocre aesthetic foundations, self-inflicted usability flaws, guideline authors who flip-flopped on their own rules every three years to harvest promotion credits for mid-to-high-level managers, and all the destructive migration costs dumped squarely on external developers.

01 | A Complete Collapse

If a design system were truly as brilliant as its launch keynotes claimed, the most damning metric twelve years on is simple: how many people are actually still using it?

Lay out the cold facts from official announcements, Git commit logs, and third-party metrics, and what emerges is not an industry benchmark, but an abandoned open-source junkyard:

Open-source cross-platform libraries in full retreat:

iOS: In July 2021, the official MDC-iOS repository posted a maintenance-mode notice and wiped all its documentation off material.io overnight. The project lead publicly advised developers to just stick with Apple's native UIKit and SwiftUI.

Web: In June 2024, MDC-Web was officially deprecated, and the Material Web Components (MWC) library entered maintenance mode. The team went so far as to bluntly state: "Material 3 Expressive will not be implemented for Web."

Android Native Views: In May 2026, MDC-Android 1.14.0 shipped and was promptly frozen, with all new feature development halted.

Google's Beloved Framework, Flutter: In May 2025, the team publicly refused to write a single line of code for Expressive. By August 2026, Flutter 3.47 went further, decoupling Material entirely from the core SDK into a standalone package and announcing a pivot to a "style-agnostic core."

React Ecosystem Leader MUI: MUI, with tens of millions of downloads, kept its issue tracking MD3 support open on GitHub for five whole years. The maintainers delayed it repeatedly, eventually removed it from all roadmaps, and still keep a banner on their homepage: "Material Design 2 only."

Screenshot: MUI Issue #29345 documents five years of stagnation in third-party ecosystem adoption of MD3.

Major apps look the other way:

According to Android Studio data from October 2026, Android 12 and above now powers 77.8% of active devices worldwide. Yet after four years of aggressive marketing for wallpaper dynamic theming, WhatsApp and Telegram haven't bothered to add a single toggle. When Apple introduced a new visual design language, however, both giants adapted within months.

Hardware leaders vote with their feet:

Samsung, controlling the hardware gateway for most Android users worldwide, flatly refused to adopt Expressive in One UI 8, giving Google zero leeway.

Marginalized web icon assets:

In the web icon library market, Material Icons and Material Symbols combined hold a measly 3.5% market share, while third-party Font Awesome dominates with 88.3%.

From the systemic abandonment of codebase after codebase to the frantic decoupling by Google’s own frameworks, and from hardware titans to top-tier consumer apps giving it the cold shoulder, this supposed cross-platform design language has been dead in the water for years.

02 | A Broken Infrastructure Contract

Before dissecting how ugly or unusable Material Design became, we need to get one definition straight: what does it actually mean for a design system to fail?

A design system is not a conceptual art installation built for an exhibition hall, nor is it a vanity mockup whipped up by a designer on Pinterest. Inside an operating system serving billions of people, a design system is fundamentally an engineering infrastructure contract. Its sole reason for existing is to lower collaboration costs across an entire ecosystem, smooth over the fragmentation of disparate hardware, and provide developers with a stable, durable, out-of-the-box foundation.

When a design system that marketed itself as "digital physics" winds up after twelve years in this state:

Every cross-platform promise broken by its own creators: Open-source implementations for iOS, the web, and Flutter systematically shut down one after another;

First-party teams leading the mutiny: Google’s highest-earning, highest-DAU apps preferring proprietary UIs over their own company's design system;

Platform hardware partners and top-tier ecosystems in collective resistance: Samsung pivoting to copy Apple while WhatsApp and Telegram won't even build a toggle;

Internal engineers publicly firing broadsides: Former developers who built it calling it "an objective failure" on social media;

And the captain himself expressing public regret: Matías Duarte, who introduced it to the world, admitting a decade later that its execution was "one of my biggest regrets."

Let me ask: if this doesn't qualify as a failure, what on earth does?

This isn't a "minor compromise." It is an unmitigated engineering bankruptcy and institutional collapse. Far from curing Android’s fragmentation, it dumped salt directly into the wound.

03 | Twelve Years of Self-Sabotage

Looking back at the past twelve years, Material Design’s roadmap reads like a farce: keynotes promise revolutionary breakthroughs, reality leaves behind a mess of half-baked tools, and three years later the company renames the system, trashes the previous version, and promises another revolution.

2014【Material 1.0】
├─ Pitched: Tactile paper & digital physics
└─ Reality: Eye-searing palette & contrast fails

│

▼
2018【Material Theming】
├─ Pitched: Brand customization & visual variety
└─ Reality: Bloated MDC libraries & abandoned goals

│

▼
2021【Material You】
├─ Pitched: Algorithmic color & personal emotion
└─ Reality: Muddy pastels & broken elevation

│

▼
2025【M3 Expressive】
├─ Pitched: Countercultural vibe & kill the boring
└─ Reality: Bloated controls & ecosystem pushback

2014 (Material 1.0: The Paper Illusion): Launched alongside Android 5.0 Lollipop under the banner of "quantum paper," attempting to construct visual hierarchy through 3D elevation and cast shadows. Yet the concept was so abstract that Google couldn't even deliver a competent native component library, leaving developers to discover every pitfall the hard way.

2018 (Material Theming / M2: The First Reversal): Barely four years in, Google buckled. In the official blog post Making More with Material, the team sheepishly conceded the truth: the old rules were so rigid that every app looked identical, and brands had no room to express themselves. Enter "Theming," an attempt to loosen the reins for third-party brands. But the accompanying Material Components (MDC) library was bloated and painful to migrate to. Before teams could even get their bearings, Google had already shifted the goalposts again.

2021 (Material You / M3: Sinking Deeper into the Mud): Shipped with Android 12. Digital paper physics went out the window, replaced by algorithmic color extraction from wallpapers ("Monet"), claiming to hand color choices to users. The algorithm proved notoriously erratic, washing system palettes out in dingy pastels and kicking the seven-year-old elevation shadow system to the curb in favor of "Elevation Overlays"—a tint-layer nightmare that drove frontend and mobile developers up the wall.

2025 (M3 Expressive: Off the Rails): On the eve of Android 16, Google ran the exact same playbook. In an official post-mortem, the team admitted that a 2022 internal study found their own apps "too similar, too boring," prompting the release of Expressive. This new iteration bloated controls to comical sizes and tuned animation easing curves into sluggish molasses. This time, the ecosystem didn't even pretend to play along: the Web team refused to adopt it, Flutter refused to write code for it, and Samsung simply ignored it.

Four generations in twelve years. Not once did a new generation fix the technical debt of the last; instead, it tore up past promises, piled on breaking changes, and left developers holding the bag.

04 | Aesthetic Flaws: From Garish Clashing to Corner Chaos

You can't critique a design system without talking about aesthetics. Let's be blunt: compared to Apple, Google's design language has always suffered from an inescapable plastic cheapness.

Apple’s designs have had their share of controversies (from ultra-thin fonts in iOS 7 to the blurred translucency of Liquid Glass), but they rest on rigorous typography engines, Retina anti-aliasing calibration, disciplined lighting tiers, and deep typesetting traditions. Google’s team, by contrast, has never seemed to understand restraint or refinement.

Garish Saturation and Contrast Failures

Pull up the early official color palette from Material 1.0 in 2014, and the scheme once treated as gospel looks like an unmitigated visual disaster.

Back then, Google was obsessed with pairing eye-watering, high-saturation "Deep Purple" and "Indigo" with blinding fluorescent accents like "Pink A200." Screens were drowned in massive unmodulated swaths of flat color, looking like a retro flashback to the early 2000s color-screen flip-phone era.

Worse still was accessibility. Measured against the globally recognized W3C WCAG contrast standards, the official 2014 guidelines recommended pairing white text with Light Blue 500, yielding a contrast ratio of just 2.63:1. Cyan 500 managed a laughable 2.30:1—failing even the bare-minimum 3:1 threshold required for large bold headlines, let alone the 4.5:1 standard for body copy.

When you can't even get basic contrast math right, how do you have the gall to market your work as "the physics of the digital world"?

Image: Official UI examples from the 2014 Material 1.0 spec. The Cyan 500 header with white text on the left scores a contrast ratio of just 2.30:1 (failing WCAG’s 3:1 minimum), while the right displays the fluorescent Pink A200 floating action button heavily promoted at launch.

The Arrogance of CJK Typography

When it came to non-Latin typography—especially the massive ideographic systems of CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean)—Google's carelessness was impossible to hide.

The 2014 official typography guide dismissed CJK with an insulting one-line fix: take the Latin type scale and "add 1px to font size, add 0.1em to line height." Android 5 hadn't even bundled the full weight family for Noto Sans CJK yet; while English screens used Light and Medium weights to evoke breathability, Chinese text collapsed into an impenetrable mass of dark strokes.

To make matters worse, the guidelines forced the English "all-caps button" convention directly onto Chinese characters. Square ideographs are already self-contained geometric blocks that have no upper- or lowercase ascenders. Shoving them into all-caps styling produced bloated, awkward buttons with hollow margins and completely derailed visual balance.

Muddy Pastels and Conflicting Radii

Fast forward to Material You in 2021: paper was forgotten, and algorithmic wallpaper color extraction ("Monet") took the spotlight.

We all lived through the result. The algorithm paid zero regard to brand identity or semantic meaning, bleaching every interface in a muddy haze of dull pastels. Serious banking balances and productivity documents were forcibly bathed in drab Morandi tints. Designer @jhaverinator mocked the disjointed palettes on X with a rhyming zinger:

Half of it is red / Half of it is blue / What an inconsistent UI / Is Material You.

Screenshot: @jhaverinator's original post lampooning the jarring color splits in Material You.

Frontend and mobile developers spent months venting on forums. Under MD3’s Elevation Overlay mechanism, even if you explicitly hardcoded a card’s background to #FFFFFF, the system insisted on blending a semi-opaque tint of the primary color over it for "spatial hierarchy," leaving surfaces looking permanently soiled.

Then came the corner radii. Designer Tom Farrell (@tomfarrell_1) took to X with screenshots of the stock system UI, pointing out four or five wildly conflicting corner radii jammed into a single screen. When you can't even align basic geometric corner curves within your own OS, how do you publish Medium think pieces lecturing the world on design craft?

Screenshot: @tomfarrell_1's original post pointing out conflicting corner radii coexisting within the system UI.

By 2025, M3 Expressive abandoned all restraint: controls bloated to swallow half the screen, and spring animations dragged like cold honey. As one Hacker News commenter put it: "People use phones to get things done, not to tap on a giant kiosk at a train station."

05 | Interaction Disasters: Self-Indulgence as Spec

Beyond visual misfires, Material's interaction models reeked of academic designers operating on unchecked arrogance.

The Hamburger Drawer Trap

Early Material treated the navigation drawer like holy scripture. Every app, regardless of architecture, was instructed to tuck primary navigation behind those three little horizontal bars in the top-left corner.

All in the name of a clean canvas, essential navigation was banished out of sight. The cost? Every single time users wanted to switch sections, they had to reach for the farthest corner of the screen, wait for the drawer to slide out, scan the list, and tap—adding layers of interaction friction to everyday tasks.
